newsitem.title: CHINA: Shenzhen exchange bids for top China spot.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen exchange bids for top China spot.

text.p: Shenzhen's stock exchange has thrown down the gauntlet to its big brother in Shanghai by declaring its aim to be China's best bourse and a world-class market within 20 years, official media said on Friday.

Analysts said the bourse was intent on overcoming a perception in the market that it could be overshadowed by the much larger exchange in Hong Kong after the colony reverts to Chinese control next year.

"We aim to build ourselves into the bourse with the lowest trading costs in China through the use of high technology," the China Securities newspaper quoted its president, Zhuang Xinyi, as telling a meeting of the exchange's 700 members.
"We aim to provide the highest quality services, the best computer systems and become the best regulated market in the country," he said.
Not content with becoming number one in China, Zhuang said Shenzhen wanted to become a world-standard exchange in the next 15 to 20 years.

"We will make the bourse rank among the world's major securities market in such areas as variety of securities, trading volume, number of listed firms, members and investors and risk control systems reaching the level of the world's advanced markets," Zhuang said.
Over the past few months, Shenzhen has overtaken Shanghai in turnover of domestic A share trading and capitalisation of foreign currency B shares.
China has said it has no plan for a third bourse at least before Hong Kong is taken over on July 1 next year.
Analysts said Zhuang's speech was evidence of Shenzhen's efforts to keep growing and avert a possible crisis of identity over its future role after Hong Kong reverts to China.
They said they believed that it appeared Beijing was happy to allow Shenzhen to continue to grow up to and beyond next year's Chinese takeover of Hong Kong.
But analysts said it was still unclear how the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hong Kong stock markets would interact in the longer term.
"Zhuang's speech aims to boost morale and reflects the exchange's sense of crisis," said one stock analyst with a major Chinese securities house.
"By taking the initiative and kicking off a fresh round of competition with Shanghai and later even with Hong Kong, the exchange wants to establish a new sense of importance," he said.

"Hong Kong will continue to play the role of attracting international funds after the takeover, but with its different political system, it will not be able to divert large amounts of funds in and out of the mainland," said a second analyst.
"Investors do not care which exchange -- Shenzhen, Shanghai or Hong Kong -- wins the competition," said a third analyst. "They believe competition will help improve services and benefit investors."
Turnover and new listings on the Shenzhen exchange have grown faster than Shanghai in recent months. But Shanghai has a much larger market capitalisation.
